title: From physical problems to representation decomposition: step-by-step derivation
description: 32 guided exercises: try each problem before revealing its derivation and answer step by step. Each includes a comprehension check and a linked experiment. New topics include exact S₃ probabilities for higher-dimensional inputs, five-path counting with input 15, dimension-reduced coefficients and exact complex states with input 27, and Casimir two-body energies for inequivalent representations.

exercises.title: SU(2) · Derivation of π pulse from exponential matrix
exercises.prompt: Starting from |↑⟩ under resonance conditions, find the time for the first complete transfer to |↓⟩ and interpret the final phase.
givens: H/ℏ=Ωσx/2，Ω>0；σx²=I
exercises.hint: Divide the exponential series into even powers and odd powers. First find the state amplitude, and then take the square of the modulus.

steps.title: Write exponents as trigonometric functions
steps.explanation: Even powers of σx equal I, while odd powers equal σx. The even terms of the exponential series sum to a cosine; the odd terms sum to −i times a sine.

steps.title: acts on the initial state
steps.explanation: Since σx|↑⟩=|↓⟩, the rotation turns one initial basis state into a coherent superposition of two basis states.

steps.title: Find the first probability of one
steps.explanation: First take the square of the absolute value of the state amplitude, and then find the minimum positive time. The sign of the amplitude cannot be used to determine whether the probability is positive or negative.

steps.title: distinguishes state vectors from measurement probabilities
steps.explanation: At this time, the amplitude of the upper state is zero and the amplitude of the lower state is −i. The overall phase alone does not change the measurement probability; if two coherent paths are compared, the relative phase needs to be tracked.

exercises.answer: is tπ=π/Ω, and the final state is −i|↓⟩. This requires the resonance, constant drive, and no decoherence conditions of this problem.
exercises.pitfall: For Δ≠0, the rotation axis is no longer x, and waiting for π/Ω generally does not produce complete inversion.

choices: 4π
check.explanation: is directly substituted into tπ=π/Ω; the time unit is the reciprocal of the used angular frequency unit.

exercises.title: SU(3) · Check 27-dimensional representation from Dynkin tags
exercises.prompt: Find the dimension, conjugate label and quadratic Casimir of (p,q)=(2,2), and determine whether these numbers are energies.
givens: C₂(p,q)=[p²+q²+pq+3p+3q]/3
uses the normalization of Tₐ=λₐ/2; the conjugation labels are (q,p)
exercises.hint: Calculate the dimension and Casimir separately and do not confuse them with the dimension of the group itself.

steps.title: Find the dimension of the representation space
steps.explanation: The three factors are 3, 3, and 6; divide their product by 2. The resulting number counts independent states in the representation space.

steps.title: Find the quadratic Casimir
steps.explanation: Add the square term, mixed term, and linear term separately, and the sum is 24.

steps.title: Check conjugation
steps.explanation: still gets (2,2) after swapping p and q, so this representation is equivalent to its own conjugate.

steps.title: gives the result the correct physical meaning
steps.explanation: 27 is representation dimension and 8 is this normalized Casimir eigenvalue; neither gives the energy directly. If a model also has H=aC₂+bI, the energy can be calculated from its coefficients.
steps.formula: E=8a+b only when H=aC₂+bI is given

exercises.answer: (2,2) is the 27-dimensional representation of the self-conjugate, C₂=8. The real dimension of the SU(3) group is still 8, which is exactly the same as the Casimir value here is just a numerical coincidence of different concepts.
exercises.pitfall: The same conjugation label indicates self-conjugation; conversely, it cannot be assumed that two representations are equivalent just because they have the same dimensions.

check.question: Both 3 and 3̄ have quadratic Casimir 4/3. What does this imply?
choices: They must be equivalent representations
quadratic Casimir cannot distinguish between these two representations on its own
They are all four-dimensional representations
check.explanation: label (1,0) is different from (0,1); quadratic Casimir is invariant under p,q exchange.

exercises.title: SU(3) · Derivation of 3⊗3̄ from the trace of the matrix
exercises.prompt: Identify 3⊗3̄ with the space of complex 3×3 matrices. Prove that it contains a singlet and find the dimension of the remaining subspace.
givens: M→UMU†，U∈SU(3)
Tr(UMU†)=Tr M；UIU†=I
matrix space is 3×3=9
exercises.hint: Split an arbitrary matrix into a multiple of the identity and a traceless part.

steps.title: Isolate the invariant direction
steps.explanation: identity matrix direction is invariant under all conjugate transformations, so this dimensional space is trivial representation .

steps.title: Construct the traceless part
steps.explanation: subtracts the trace direction to get M₀. The conjugate transformation still keeps its trace zero, so this eight-dimensional subspace is closed to the group action.

steps.title: Identify the adjoint representation
steps.explanation: The conjugation action on traceless matrices is the complexified adjoint representation, of dimension 9−1=8. The original tensor-product space therefore splits into 1 and 8.

steps.title: Normalize singlets and interpret indicators
steps.explanation: The three diagonal bases are orthogonal, and the equal coefficients are added and then normalized by 1/√3. When the index is taken as color, this is the color singlet of quark-antiquark; when it is taken as flavor, it is the flavor singlet.

exercises.answer: The trace direction gives one normalized singlet; the remaining traceless space is the eight-dimensional adjoint representation, with 9=1+8. Interpret color and flavor singlets according to their respective indices.
exercises.pitfall: If the second factor is 3 instead of 3̄, the transformation is no longer M→UMU† and this trace proof cannot be followed.

check.question: 3⊗3 Is 1⊕8 also obtained from this trace argument?
choices: Yes, because the dimension is also 9
Yes, just change one coordinate axis
check.explanation: The tensor of the two basic indicators is divided into symmetric and antisymmetric parts, and the result is 6⊕3̄, without singlets.

steps.title: First combine the first two factors
steps.explanation: is 6, and the anti-symmetric channel is 3̄. The product space dimension is 6+3=9.

steps.title: Continue along both channels
steps.explanation: adds a third 3 to channel 6 to produce 10 and 8; adding a third 3 to channel 3̄ produces another 8 and 1.

steps.title: Retain multiplicities and check dimensions
steps.explanation: The two octets are equivalent representations in independent subspaces. They contribute 16 states; neither copy may be deleted.

steps.explanation: The color singlet is the sum ε_{abc}|a b c⟩/√6, a fully antisymmetric combination. Flavor multiplets must additionally be analyzed together with spin, orbital degrees of freedom, and fermionic statistics.

exercises.answer: resolves to 10⊕8⊕8⊕1. The two octets are from the middle 6 and 3̄ coupling channels respectively; this representation count alone does not predict the true baryon mass.

exercises.title: SU(3) · The boundary between the octet direct product and selection rule
exercises.prompt: Check the dimensionality of 8⊗8, exchange symmetry partitions, and determine whether "group theory allows" is sufficient to determine the transition rate.
givens: If the operator is transformed according to R_{op}, non-zero matrix elements require R_f contained in R_{op}⊗R_i
exercises.hint: Count the total dimension, then the exchange-symmetric and exchange-antisymmetric spaces. Finally separate representation constraints from dynamics.

steps.title: Check the total dimensions and multiplicity
steps.explanation: Both octets contribute 8 each and must be counted together. The two ten-dimensional terms have different conjugate labels but the same number of dimensions.

steps.title: Check exchange symmetry space
steps.explanation: The symmetric square dimension is n(n+1)/2, and the antisymmetric square dimension is n(n−1)/2. Substitute n=8 respectively to check the two sets of results.

steps.title: explains the extra tags for the two octets
steps.explanation: 8s and 8a are both representations of highest weight (1,1); s/a describes the properties of exchanging two factors. The tensor product decomposition of multiplicity alone cannot construct the state-wise CG basis of these subspaces.
steps.formula:
SU(3) Same type: (1,1)
Exchange eigenvalues are different: +1 vs. −1

steps.title: Testing the scope of physical inferences
steps.explanation: An octet operator acting on an octet initial state has two reduced coupling channels to an octet final state. Whether a transition occurs and its strength still depend on dynamics and other quantum numbers. Total exchange symmetry of identical particles must also include spin and spatial parts.
steps.formula: R_f⊂R_{op}⊗R_i is a necessary condition and the transition rate is not given.

exercises.answer: The total dimension is 64, with symmetric/antisymmetric dimensions 36/28. The two octets are independent equivalent representations. Representation selection rules exclude forbidden channels but do not replace matrix-element calculations.
exercises.pitfall: You cannot regard 8s and 8a as new SU(3) irreducible types, nor can you ignore the remaining degrees of freedom and delete 8a just because the particle is a boson.

check.question: selection rule allows a channel, but the corresponding reduced matrix element is zero, what is the conclusion?
choices: still must transition
The channel amplitude is still zero
The group theory decomposition must be wrong
check.explanation: Representation containment is only a necessary condition for a possibly nonzero matrix element. Dynamics can make an allowed channel's matrix element exactly zero.
